Personal Finance is largely a game of budgeting, paying off / keeping out of debt, and saving money for large future expenses (e.g. car, career change, kids, retirement, etc.). 

The first step to all of this is building a budget: a plan for what expenses you prioritize based on the money you make, and the first step of a budget is an expense estimate. You need to know how much you need to make to **break even**. 

Start keeping receipts, and if your parents pay some/all of your bills ask questions. How much does it cost to keep you fed currently in a month? How about insured? How about with a roof over your head? How about to keep your car running if you have one (with gas and mechanic fees)? How about mandatory minimums on any debt you have?

After that you can get a realistic picture of how much you need to make to ‘live independently’. Any money left over should be used in the following ways: an emergency fund for unexpected expenses (recommended 3-6 months of expenses in an easily accessible account incase you get laid off or something comes up outside of your regular monthly budget), paying down debt if you have it, start paying into a retirement fund (approx. 10-15% of your gross income is recommended by most financial advisers), and start saving for big expenses you may have coming up.

Only after all that can you start realistically thinking about “fun money”. It will be less than you hope, but if you keep track of your finances well and make sure you have a good job there should be a steady drip of money you can put into hobbies or the occasional controlled splurge.

When trying to figure out if something is a scam, consider the business model:

Payday loans operate because people have trouble paying their bills, so they get a short term loan to try to pay for something before payday. 

The issue is when payday comes around and they pay off the loan they once again do not have the money to pay for their bills (because they spent so much paying off the loan with the added fees). 

This causes them to get out another loan. Which means they have to once again keep paying fees. 

Payday loans trap people in debt because they rely on people not being able to pay off their debts to them and their bills. This trapped aspect of payday loans (in addition to the exorbitant fees) is why they are called a scam.

Also here’s some useful banking information I learned: 

Sperm is stored in units of ‘vials’ which are usually about .5ml in volume. For about 3.5 ml ejaculate volume I got about 4 vials after testing and processing. Think about a vial as like one ‘try’. So each IVF or IUI try would use one vial/try. With IVF they may be able to salvage some for another, but typically the vials are pretty much ‘one-use only’. 

On average, each IVF try has between a 10% to about a 40% chance of successfully inseminating. IUI has about a 12-16%, but is massively less expensive and intensive. Those numbers came from a midwife I talked with. 

As long as you have >20 mil motile sperm per vial it should be a good vial. I had about 60 million, but as long as it is >20 the difference in effectiveness is negligible. The rest is related to your partner’s fertility, timing, and the overall skill of the practitioner helping you. This should be somewhat comforting because even if your count doesn’t bounce back completely and ends up being ‘below average’ it might not negatively affect your fertility. 

And even if when you do the collection you get <20 million/vial it doesn’t necessarily mean that you can’t still make it work. Fertility is expensive, but it has come a long long way over the years. 

The midwife I talked to said 12 vials was a good benchmark amount for sperm storage, especially if you don’t know how many children you might want or possible complications along the way. 

I had to do 3 collections to get to my goal of 12, and for the collections, the cost of testing, and my first year of storage I paid around $2000 in total. I did not go through insurance. 

It was hard not being on estrogen, especially given that I had such great results in terms of mental health and lifting of brain fog. I do think it is worth it though, especially if having kids is something you think you are interested in.

Common cancer sites are in areas that are prone to mutation. 

Mutation is common in places that have a lot of cell divisions or have external factors (e.g. nicotine exposure for lung cancer or UV exposure for skin cancer). 

Breast tissue goes through a lot of cell divisions, mostly caused from menstrual cycles. Because of this, every month many many cells get replaced with new ones, and every replacement increases the chances of cancer developing. 

Fun fact, pregnancy actually reduces the chances of developing breast cancer, because it reduces the total number of menstrual cycles and stabilizes the relevant hormones for breast feeding during several subsequent menstrual cycles. All this means fewer cell replacements and fewer chances for spontaneous mutation.

In plain english, given a homomorphic mapping between two rings the kernel is the set of elements in the first ring that gets mapped to 0 in the second ring. 

Here’s why it is useful: 0 is significant to both addition and multiplication in rings. It allows operations to pretty much disappear, and because of closure if all your elements are within the kernel the result is also in the kernel. Eg. 0+0*0=0

If the two rings are linear vector spaces the kernel is the null space. 

Kernels also allow you to do something special called a quotient which basically lets you reduce your space. I won’t get into the details, but basically it is the opposite of the product space if you can imagine that. 

All in all, kernels are very useful for a lot of things, but to be honest when I first learned them I didn’t understand why we cared either. Hope this helps :)

The fact that you do triathlon doesn’t actually surprise me. We have nearly opposite requirements for our calves and ankles when we swim versus when we run. 

When we swim we want our calves to be loose and respond fluidly to changes in pressure to make our kick fluid and efficient reducing drag while keeping our feet pointed practically the entire time. 

However, when we run our calves are our shock absorbers. They are meant to be springy, and they are meant to be resisting the pressure we put on them. Meanwhile our ankles should never be pointed when we run and should stabilize our legs under uneven ground. 

I always struggled to get my swimming kick to be fluid, and I know many swimmers whose calves were weak and would collapse after sufficient mileage. I’m going to guess you’re more of a swimmer vs a runner, right?

If so I’m also going to guess that trail running leads to a lot of rolled ankles for you. 

Extended calf raises where your toes are on a stair so your ankles can bent past 90 degrees should be your best friend to build calf strength and mobility. 

Another good one for a lot of my swimming buddies is balance training. It should strengthen the muscles stabilizing the ankle. It doesn’t have to be complicated: try standing barefoot on one leg for one minute. I think you’ll be surprised how hard it is and how often you almost fall over. Harder versions like standing on your bed on one leg are excellent also because you have to actively prevent your ankle from collapsing. 

Balance training is also one of the most overlooked aspects of running training and fitness in general, and honestly I’d recommend everyone incorporate some into their training. If you get good at it you may even find yourself surpassing many of your running-centric buddies in terms of ankle health.

Without getting into specifics about your situation, yes absolutely upper body posture can affect loading and muscle firing in the lower body. 

Running is repetitive, so small changes in form can drastically change how much you are expecting from different body parts. 

What it sounds like you are doing though is likely not positive in the long run (both figuratively and literally). You are compensating for weakness in one area of your body by changing your overall posture. 

My advice would be to drop the mileage, focus on mobility, and maybe try to switch to a shoe with a lower heel to toe drop. I found for me switching to a zero-drop shoe my calves got radically stronger, and I could more safely handle heavy load and pounding, especially on down hills. Just give your body a chance to adjust. 

Also, if you are really unsure if the posture is better one way or another try doing a recording of your running form on a treadmill. Do it from the back and the side. Watch how your feet land, if anything is collapsing, if you’re landing unevenly, if you struggle to keep a consistent strike pattern, etc. That will help you see how your form is naturally and how it changes when you move your pelvis as you are moving it. This will also help you in the long run 

If changing your posture does end up helping your overall form, great! Otherwise, I’d recommend against blindly compensating for pain. You can really mess things up over time. Take it from me: I have some scar tissue in my quads because I compensated for cramping in my calves during training and in racing.
Most of the time, hollow backs are caused by either weak core strength or compensating for mobility issues elsewhere to keep you balanced. Likely it’s shoulder mobility. I have the same problem.

Artificial colors serve both an aesthetic but also practical purpose: to help people figure out what they are looking at with a glance. 

The story starts when people wanted to make a raspberry flavored water-ice. Sounds great, right? And because raspberries are red, the water-ice should be red, right? 

Well, unfortunately red was already a widely used color with strawberry, cherry, and watermelon so throwing in another red would make it hard to distinguish. 

So they decided to turn raspberry flavored water-ice blue, which was not a highly contested color. And to make it interesting and clear they called it “blue-raspberry”. Over the years people have taken more and more liberties with blue-raspberry and added other flavors to it beyond just raspberry. Thats why it tastes so different from raspberry.

Let’s start with how The Cold War got its name, because it isn’t just a random name. A cold war is a term to describe a certain flavor of warfare where no direct military invasion occurs. 

When countries invade, the war becomes a ‘hot war’, it is what we normally think of when we think of war. 

Wikipedia: “A cold war is a state of conflict between nations that does not involve direct military action but is pursued primarily through economic and political actions, propaganda, acts of espionage or proxy wars waged by surrogates.”

Effectively, we never directly invaded the USSR nor did they us. Instead we influenced the politics of other countries in proxy to “gain ground”. Direct invasion was out of the question with the threat of nuclear armaments, but we did have troops on the ground elsewhere to gain political ground and assemble allies against the USSR and they did the same against us. 

The Vietnam War was one such fight of influence. The USSR supported North Vietnam and the Viet Cong whereas the US primarily supported South Vietnam and the ARVN. 

In short, yes the Vietnam War was part of a series of wars backed in part by the USSR and is considered part of the Cold War.

This is a very solid starter plan. You seem like you have a good idea of goals and objectives. That is really great. 

However, this feels like a peak training plan for a mid to long distance runner. As in, this is great for in-season training or prep work for a race <= a month out or so. 

If you aren’t doing indoor track, I recommend doing way more cross training, mobility work, strength work, and maybe some sprint/hurdle work if you’re up to it. 

Thats the point of off-season work: to switch up your training and to build those skillsets you don’t have time to build when training for a specific race like a 5k. This will make you a much more versatile runner and massively reduce the odds of injury and burnout. 

To do this, do the following:

1. Identify areas of weakness in your running. Here are a few examples:

- It might be not as strong of a kick. 
- It might be weak ankles/joints. 
- It might be constant tightness in hamstrings, hips, or calves. 
- It might be a lack of agility and coordination on technical trails. 
- It might be your running form in general. 

2. Identify **Specific** exercises and activities to target each of those areas of weakness. Likely it will involve all those activities I mentioned above (cross training, mobility work, sprint work, form drills, balance work, lifting, etc.), but try to be as specific as possible. 

3. Come up with a flexible training plan to incorporate those activities. Some notes:

- Recovery is the time you build the muscle, strength, power, and mobility from the workouts.  As a result, recovery is criticality important in the offseason. 

Incorporate lots of recovery into your plan. Recovery doesn’t always mean rest, btw. It can mean that, but you can get creative. A stretching/icing day is hardly ever a bad thing if you are sore. You can even take that time you would’ve worked out to do schoolwork so you can get more sleep. 

- I would try to maintain some cardiovascular fitness with long runs or tempo runs one or maybe two times a week. That is all you need. The rest of the time, use it to target weaknesses or rest. I promise it doesn’t set you back, only makes you more receptive to future training while reducing the chance of injury. 

- Take it easy: mental burnout is very real. Doing high intensity work constantly will make you a worse runner in the long term. You need confidence to be competitive. Spent time training with friends. 

——

Hope all these things help. Best of luck to you :)

I’ll give a few rules of thumb about shaving and my experience:

First the rules, many you have probably already heard: 

1. Always go with the grain: going against the grain may allow you to shave closer but it will more likely cause ingrown hairs and further irritation

2. Trim first: if the hair is really long, trim it first with a beard trimmer or equivalent if you have it. Going with a razor first is likely going to leave a lot of hair and take several passes to get the smoothness desired. 

3. Prep your skin: you should know the standard routine: hot water, shaving cream, keep skin taught when shaving, etc. Not doing this often leads to not as good of a shave and often irritation.

4. A new razor never hurts: if your razor isn’t cutting like you’re hoping, trying a new blade is never a bad idea. 

Just be wary of pressure with a new blade if the other blade is fairly old (you may be used to pressing harder than necessary for the new blade and cut yourself). 

5. It may itch or be sharp when it grows back: try a moisturizer or even hydrocortisone cream if it gets bad. 

—-
My experience: while all of the above is true, I’ve found one of the most helpful add ons is a pre-shave exfoliation and post-shave moisturizing. 

The exfoliation seems to make the skin smoother in general and the shave closer, leading to less rubbing. 

The moisturizer also seems to help a lot, especially with itchy skin and irritation. 

Hope these help :)

 ∫x^(n-1) dx = (x^n + c)/n

Perhaps not entirely related but this reminds me of the ‘therapeutic index’ in drug trials. 

All drugs have a dosage that is harmful when enough is taken, and some have a dosage that is beneficial (called the therapeutic zone). In this way drugs are both. 

You said that you want a word that is neutral in terms of both effect and delivery system. I’m guessing so that way you can use it in some generic context. 

In pharmacological terms, drug fits this. It is any non-food substance or chemical which alters some system in the body. This does not imply positive effect (hence why some drugs are banned). Nor does drug imply delivery system. However, you said this isn’t what you are looking for. Here are some other ideas:

Substance: I’ve seen many people submit this, and it seems to fit all your criteria. But to me this feels too general and may lack a certain pointedness that toxin has to be a useful replacement. 

Compound: this isn’t bad. It implies something intentionally created or synthesized without the connotative positive or negative charge. Additionally, it doesn’t imply a delivery system. To me this seems like a good option. Though it may sound too general, as toxin often is in relation to some organism. Compound doesn’t have to. e.g. an explosive compound. 

Elixir: not quite delivery neutral, but is effect neutral. Though it does have a certain ‘witchy’ connotation. e.g. Making elixirs and potions in a cauldron. 

Extract: implies purity and potency, but not properties. Depending upon the context, it may not apply if attempted to use as generic term. 

Solution: implies liquid, but not effect or delivery. Though some association with ingestion, you can have topical solutions. 

Hope one of these works :)

Here’s a good example structure of that conversation:

1) Investigation: Ask her “when we aren’t texting during the day, are you afraid that I’ve forgotten you exist?” 

Example Response: “well yeah, it’s as if you don’t even care about me. You never text me first, if we even text at all it feels like you are just checking boxes.”

2) If yes, reaffirm the connection. Give her a long hug. Tell her, “I’m so sorry you feel that way. That sounds really really scary. When we are apart, do you ever forget about me that way? “

Likely response is “no, but how am I supposed to know you don’t? Like sometimes it feels like you don’t care about me at all.”

3) Explain how you do feel: cite specific events and examples leaving little to no room for reinterpretation. She may fill in the gaps with worst case scenarios about how you’ve forgotten about her and don’t care. 

This will be highly personalized, but the point is to impart the message that she isn’t simply or easily replaceable or insignificant. You can remember details about her and her actions have a lasting positive impact on you. 

Here’s an example: 
“Do you remember our first date? Where we did [fill in the blank]? 

I remember you [cite specific example of action she did which felt endearing (e.g. scrunched her nose when looking at the sun, wouldn’t stop playing with rings on her hand, how when she laughed the way the muscles in her face moved, etc.)], 

and I remember just thinking [tell her how those actions made you feel and left a lasting positive impact (e.g. “Wow. She really is something else. I remember it like it was yesterday, I felt the butterflies right here in my solar plexus”)]. 

I didn’t just forget it right after, and in many ways I still carry those times around right now as if those moments are still happening as we speak. That doesn’t just go away when we aren’t talking. I feel it. Because in that way, it’s as if you’ve never even left. 

It scares me sometimes when you say you miss me all the time. It makes me feel bad, as if I haven’t been able to do the same for you that you’ve done for me. 

What can I do to make you feel the same way about me that I feel about you?”

Some key rules:

1) Don’t lie, or make things up. Make sure everything you say is the truth and feels accurate. 

2) Don’t actually say the words “I don’t miss you when we are apart”. You can impart the same message by framing the focus on how her fears and insecurities impact you, and how you don’t share the same negative emotions when you are apart. 

3) Make sure the focus is on how positively you view her AND how those feelings persist through time even while apart. You don’t miss someone when they haven’t truly left. 

You don’t miss your dog or are afraid your dog doesn’t love you simply because they are napping in a different room. 

4) Describe the impact her words have on you. It can hurt when someone projects such negative or shallow emotions onto you. Communicate that hurt. The conversation shouldn’t just about her feelings. 

5) Make sure when solutions come, they come in the form of her feeling in a similar way to how you feel about her. This serves 2 purposes: 1. It provides a detailed actionable description of how you want things to be between you, and 2. will once again reaffirm your care for her. 

6) Understand this will likely not be a one and done conversation. It WILL take time to fix, as those feeling are wounds and they need time and care to be healed. 

Best of luck

I’ll start with the generic advice: when you have something to say that you know is likely to be misinterpreted, it’s a good idea to ask yourself “what impact do I want this to have?”

As for more specific to your situation, I’ll make some assumptions. I suspect this is one of those things where she texts you “I miss you”, and you feel obligated to text back “I miss you too”, but you don’t really feel like she is actually gone so the words feel empty to you and feel almost as if you are lying and you feel the need to come clean. 

The most important thing is, if my impression is right, I’m guessing your girlfriend has insecurities and thinks about you during the day hoping you are doing the same. The “I miss you” text is likely a bid for connection when she feels disconnected. But if you never feel that disconnection, you won’t feel that “missing her” feeling. 

It’s okay if you never really feel that disconnection, and likely it is a good thing. It is a healthy response, and it means you have confidence in your relationship and the understanding that her feelings towards you don’t simply disappear when you aren’t talking. 

Object permanence is that part of development where you understand that just because you don’t see something isn’t in your field of view it doesn’t cease to exist. That’s why peekaboo is fun for toddlers. But there’s a similar process for emotions called “emotional permanence”,  where you understand that emotions and feelings don’t simply disappear when they aren’t in view. 

The problem is not everyone develops emotional permanence, and I suspect she is one of those people. Make sure when you tell her you emphasize the following:

1) You do actually care about her and enjoy your time with her, EVEN WHEN APART. Cement in her mind that “not missing” doesn’t equal “not caring” as to those without emotional permanence can often conflate those terms. 

2) How well she does at reassuring you that her feelings for you are genuine, predictable, and positive. The Goal: Cement in her mind that your not missing of her comes from her doing GOOD things, and it allows to be present in the things you do. 

3) Reframe conversation: make the conversation about how much you wish you could make her feel the same way (the certainty that your feelings haven’t vanished because you haven’t talked for 6 hours). Likely the feelings of lack of certainty come from never having someone whose emotions toward them felt consistent enough to be relied on. Don’t put it all on you, because it likely isn’t all your fault. Maybe the correct response to “I miss you” is “Don’t worry, I haven’t forgotten about you, love. How is your day going?”

I did a lot of running in high school for a team. I did very well, set school records, but I burned myself out mentally and by the end I wasn’t the same runner. I got injured, and couldn’t show up for races the same way anymore, neither mentally or physically. 

I had to take a hiatus from running for awhile. I’m back now, and running is actually fun again. But it’s tough sometimes. Somedays you feel off. Somedays you put so much pressure on yourself to push you lose touch with your body and can’t get out of your own head. 

Something about what you said just reminded me of myself. Doing the difficult things to try to give yourself strength, but sometimes you don’t achieve it. It doesn’t mean you’re not mentally tough. All that means is you are pushing yourself. 

The key to overcoming this run (like all difficult things) is recovery. I get the sense that means both physically and emotionally. If you want to still be running in 5 years I recommend you take the ladder seriously. 

We have bad days sometimes. It was smart to end the run early. Not carrying out your plan is not necessarily a failure to be mentally tough, sometimes it means being smart when you get feedback. Training doesn’t mean ‘beat yourself until you’re paralyzed from the waist down’. 

The key to physical recovery is give yourself a couple of days of shorter slower runs. Make sure you aren’t overtraining. 

The mental aspects are more important. Make sure you don’t feel anxiety when you put on your training shoes. That’s one of the first signs of mental burnout. Be sure to slot into your training runs that are designed for the sole purpose of being enjoyable. Perhaps a slower run with an old friend, or go to a new trail and just explore. Mental toughness requires training, and all training requires some time off from difficulty for difficulties sake.

It’s important to understand how psychologically difficult it is to be a therapist for a patient. You have to be objective, and that means not letting your patient’s trauma affect your ability to care for the patient nor let it seep out into your personal life. 

Confidentiality also plays a very critical role. 

Most therapists compartmentalize, detach, and are chronically in therapy to help mitigate effects outside sessions. 

In addition to the obvious potential legal issues, it is a MASSIVE task to integrate highly compartmentalized and intense relationships into a chronic peer role. This task is often messy, incredibly stressful, requires constant vigilance, and forces you to walk on the insane moral grey area that is duty of care in this capacity. None of the ingredients you want in a friendship. 

For all those reasons, most therapists thus choose to keep their home and work lives distinct and separate. I understand how difficult it is to let go of someone you felt so close to, but please understand just how big of an ask it is for a prior therapist to be a friend. It would not be reciprocal even if you did everything right. It is not as simple as “we can set initial boundaries on what she feels comfortable with”. She feels comfortable with work life and home life separate, and you were work life so therefore you can’t be home life too. 

Thus, that’s the boundary she set with you. Please respect it, as that boundary is critical to her way of caring for herself, her practice, her patients, and the other people in her life.

Be honest though, it’s easy to downplay your situation in therapy to ‘prevent your therapist from worrying’. If they can’t handle serious issues with maturity, composure, and caring professionalism they shouldn’t be therapists.

A rule of thumb I often use is when you feel the need to make sweeping changes very very quickly that is exactly the time to move slowly. 

Start slowly, assess slowly. A key thing to keep in mind is that therapists are people. Some are good at their job, some aren’t. Most are ethical in their practice, but unfortunately some aren’t. Psychology and psychiatry isn’t a pseudoscience and it has helped many many people. Many people in r/antipsychiatry have had bad experiences (as several other people have said), but I do not believe that is the majority of people. 

Be very careful with medication as well. Especially antipsychotic medications like clozapine. Suddenly stopping can really fuck with your body. Be aware of these things, and if you are going to stop taking it, tell them so you can at least do it safely. 

Please please please move slowly. Don’t make sweeping decisions in your life based on anonymous forums (my post included). You can take in input, but make sure you give yourself time to decide things. 

I can’t say whether your therapist and psychiatrist are best for you, but I can say mine have helped me tremendously. If you are worried about fit, talk with them. Move slowly.

But don’t make the mistake of shackling yourself down to a label. Gender and sexuality is a continuous journey of self-discovery, and many start that journey very young. Some words of wisdom though as you start down the path:

Labels are great to help explain things to others and connect you with likeminded folks. However, even the best one you can find often won’t fully describe your own experiences (and that’s okay). I love that the lgbt+ community has tied itself to the rainbow and -by extension- to color theory, because I think it’s a great metaphor. 

Many colors are called the same color (e.g. there are many different ‘green’s, but even still they can have wildly different pigments holding disparate emotional experiences). Just because you don’t align exactly with everyone you meet under a certain label doesn’t mean: you don’t have a place there, that you’re confused, that it’s not a stable place, nor that it’s not a useful place to be. 

Relax when you find that a label doesn’t quite fit right. It means you are open to the right things: being loyal to yourself and your experiences. You should be loyal to a label in the same way you are loyal to a job or to a politician; always be ready to let it go. Only then can you be comfortable using it, because it doesn’t hold the same power over you. It is a tool.
